A.explanation: About $1050\text{ N}$ is $1830\sin35^{\circ}$, the component of only one cable perpendicular to the wrong axis. It ignores the second side of the cable and uses sine instead of cosine for the component along $R$.

B.explanation: About $1500\text{ N}$ is less than one cable tension and cannot balance two $1830\text{ N}$ tensions pulling almost in the same direction as each other along the jib.

C.explanation: About $2100\text{ N}$ is close to $1830 / \cos35^{\circ}$ or a single tension plus a small addition. It does not add the two equal $1830\text{ N}$ components along the jib.

D.explanation: Both sides pull with $1830\text{ N}$ at $35^{\circ}$ to $R$, so $R = 2 \times 1830\cos35^{\circ} \approx 3000\text{ N}$ for equilibrium along the jib.

hints: Notice the pulley is frictionless, so the tension is the same on both sides of the pulley and equals the $1830\text{ N}$ weight.
Notice $R$ acts along the jib and each cable makes $35^{\circ}$ with the jib, so resolve each $1830\text{ N}$ tension into a component along the jib using cosine.
Add the two equal components acting opposite to $R$ to satisfy equilibrium along the jib direction: $R = 1830\cos35^{\circ} + 1830\cos35^{\circ}$.
walkthrough: The cable passes over a frictionless pulley carrying $1830\text{ N}$, so the tension $T$ is the same throughout the cable: $T = 1830\text{ N}$ on the vertical side and on the left-hand side.

For equilibrium of the cable and pulley, the force $R$ along the jib must balance the resultant of the two tension forces along that line. From the diagram each $1830\text{ N}$ tension acts at $35^{\circ}$ to the jib line.
Resolve each tension along the jib direction. The component of one tension opposite to $R$ is $T\cos35^{\circ} = 1830\cos35^{\circ}$.
There are two such sides, so $R = 2 \times 1830\cos35^{\circ} \approx 2 \times 1830 \times 0.8192 \approx 2998\text{ N}$, which is about $3000\text{ N}$ with sensible precision. This is option D.
